paragraphs: I've worked in and around Lafayette for a long time, and a farmhouse-style home on a park-like half-acre with mature oaks and genuine privacy is the kind of property that stops me mid-scroll. The combination of that setting, the open floor plan, and the quality of the updates at 3348 Walnut Lane made it clear to me this was something worth paying close attention to. When the listing came off the market after 69 days without a sale, I wanted to reach out, because I don't think that outcome reflects the property.

Sixty-nine days is long enough for a home this well-positioned to tell us something. At $904 per square foot, this listing sat at the upper end of the Lafayette premium range, and that's a number that requires a specific buyer who has been shown exactly why it's right. The peaceful cul-de-sac, the indoor-outdoor connection to those gardens and decks, the oak canopy and trail access, these are the things that justify the number. But if the marketing didn't actively build that case for the buyers who were in the market, the price felt exposed rather than supported. That's a strategy gap, not a property problem.

I've put together a short analysis of what I think happened and how I'd approach this differently. It covers the three friction points I see in the listing history, a positioning comparison against current Lafayette benchmarks, and a relaunch framework built around the specific assets this home actually has. Nothing in here is a generic playbook.

If you're already working with an agent toward a new listing, please feel free to set this aside. If you're not, I'd welcome a short conversation. No pressure, no pitch, just a chance to walk you through what I've found.

cover.tagline: The Blueprint for a Successful Sale

exec_summary.headline: A Fully Reimagined Farmhouse on a Half-Acre Cul-de-Sac Lot  -  and a Listing That Never Finished the Story
exec_summary.p1: 3348 Walnut Lane has the kind of combination that Lafayette buyers search hard to find: a high-quality remodel with a genuine open floor plan, four bedrooms on a 21,340-square-foot park-like lot with mature oaks and real privacy, in a location that puts Las Trampas Swim Club, the Lafayette-Orinda Trail, and top-rated schools within a short walk. The chef's kitchen with its breakfast bar, the custom built-ins, the wood-burning fireplace, the multiple access points to the gardens and deck  -  these are the details that buyers in this price range are specifically looking for when they've decided not to compromise.
exec_summary.p2: The listing history doesn't match those fundamentals. At $904 per square foot, the home was priced in the upper tier of the Lafayette premium range, and 69 days on market without a sale tells us the marketing never fully built the case that justified that number. A buyer at $1,995,000 needs to feel the value before they schedule a showing, not after. The setting, the privacy, the outdoor living  -  these are visual assets that standard MLS photography and a text description rarely capture at the level that moves a qualified buyer from interest to action. The strategy ran out of runway before it found its audience.
exec_summary.p3: A relaunch for this home needs to do one thing well: make the setting, the quality, and the lifestyle legible to buyers who are shopping online before they ever call an agent. This property has the assets to support its price. The next campaign needs to show them.

forensics.title: Friction #1: 69 Days and a Buyer Who Never Got the Visual
forensics.body: After 69 days on the market, buyer psychology had already shifted from curiosity to skepticism. Past the 45-day mark, the question changes from 'Is this a good home?' to 'What's wrong with it?'  -  and that stigma wasn't earned by 3348 Walnut Lane, it was created by a distribution strategy that ran out of ideas. A half-acre cul-de-sac lot with mature oaks and a genuine park-like setting is the kind of asset that photographs and aerial footage can communicate in seconds. Without that, buyers comparing listings online moved on before they understood what the lot actually felt like. The right buyer was likely out there during those 69 days. The listing just never reached them in a way that made them stop.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's Sky Tour captures the lot position, the oak canopy, and the cul-de-sac setting from the air  -  giving buyers the spatial context that ground photography and satellite thumbnails simply can't deliver.

forensics.title: Friction #2: A $904/Sqft Price With No Story Behind It
forensics.body: At $904 per square foot, this home sat at the top of the Lafayette premium tier. That number is defensible  -  the lot size, the quality of the remodel, the farmhouse character, and the location genuinely support it. But a buyer comparing this against other Lafayette listings at similar price points needs to understand specifically what they're getting here that they can't find elsewhere. The listing described the features. It didn't build the argument for the price. When buyers can't answer that question themselves, they move on or they offer less. The perceived value gap wasn't a pricing error  -  it was a marketing gap that left a well-priced home vulnerable to doubt.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's Zillow Showcase placement positions this home with an enhanced listing page and premium narrative placement  -  so buyers see the case for the number before they compare it to anything else.

forensics.title: Friction #3: Stale Listing, No Pivot
forensics.body: The listing was withdrawn after 69 days without a visible change in strategy  -  no media rebuild, no repositioning, no new approach. When a listing isn't working past the 45-day mark, more time on the same path doesn't rebuild buyer interest, it deepens the perception that something is wrong. A home like this, with genuine premium assets and no structural issues to explain the outcome, needed a different campaign, not just more calendar days. Passive relisting resets the clock but doesn't reset the narrative. The home deserved a real second chapter.

positioning_table.verdict: At $904/sqft versus a benchmark range of $850-$920/sqft, this home sits near the upper end of that range. At $904 per square foot, this home sits near the high end of the Lafayette premium tier, and the lot size, remodel quality, and cul-de-sac setting fully justify the position. The challenge wasn't the number  -  it was that the marketing didn't arm buyers with the visual and narrative evidence to feel confident at that price before scheduling a showing. A relaunch that leads with the lot, the setting, and the quality of the updates changes that dynamic.

pillars.title: Pillar I  -  Lead With the Half-Acre, Not the Floor Plan
pillars.body: Most buyers searching in this price range have already toured their share of updated kitchens. What they can't find easily is 21,340 square feet of park-like privacy on a cul-de-sac, within walking distance of trails and top-rated schools. That lot is the headline, and it needs to be the first thing a buyer experiences  -  from the air, from the garden, from the deck. BrightWork's Sky Tour and cinematic photography rebuild that story from the ground up, so buyers arrive at the floor plan already sold on the setting.

pillars.title: Pillar II  -  Rebuild the Narrative Before It Hits Zillow
pillars.body: The $1,995,000 ask is a number that requires preparation, not just placement. Before this home relists publicly, the case for the price needs to be built into every element of the campaign  -  the listing description, the visual sequence, the data framing, the portal presentation. BrightWork's 3D Matterport tour lets serious buyers walk every room from anywhere, reducing wasted showings and increasing the quality of the interest that actually comes through the door. Buyers who've already experienced the home online show up ready to make decisions.

pillars.title: Pillar III  -  Find the Buyer Who Was Never Reached
pillars.body: The buyer for this home is likely a Lafayette-focused professional or family that's been circling Lamorinda from San Francisco or Oakland, shopping online before committing to a weekend of showings. They weren't necessarily inactive during those 69 days  -  they just weren't being reached by a standard MLS distribution. BrightWork's geo-targeted digital campaigns put this home in front of Bay Area buyers who are actively researching Lafayette before they've found what they're looking for, turning passive searchers into scheduled showings.
